--- title: "Fonts in ggplot" subtitle: "Using fonts in ggplot and on your website" date: 2025/8/02 date-modified: today order: 20 bibliography: - grateful-refs.bib fig-align: center --- ## {{< iconify noto-v1 package >}} Setting up R Packages ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(ggformula) library(sysfonts) ## use custom fonts (need to be installed on your OS) library(systemfonts) # Thomas Pederson's recent font management package library(showtext) ## add google fonts to plots library(ggtext) ## add improved text rendering to ggplot2 ## library(ggrepel) ## Text-repelled labels library(marquee) ## Annotations with fonts in ggplot ``` ::: We may have been using `ggplot2` for a while now, but there is always more to learn about the aesthetics of our plots. In this module, we will explore how to use different fonts and themes to make our plots look more polished and professional. We may also want to use fonts on our websites and we will look at using packages like `sysfonts` . `gfonts`, and `showtext` to add custom fonts to our plots and websites. For instance you may want your website to look this: [Project Peasants](https://project-peasants.netlify.app) !! ## Using Preferred Fonts We may prefer specific fonts for **our plots**, and we may also want to use these fonts on our websites. There are (atleast) two steps to using fonts in R: 1. Setting up the Fonts 1. Using them in ggplot and on your website. Let us look at both these steps! ### Option 1: Live-loading Fonts from Google The easiest way to get fonts is **live downloading of fonts** from Google using the `sysfonts` package. These are then easily added within the R session using the `showtext` package. Head off view to [Google Fonts](https://fonts.google.com/) and select the fonts you might want to work with. Let us add a handful of fonts to our R session. We will use the `sysfonts::font_add_google()` function from the `sysfonts` package to download Google fonts into our session. These fonts will then be included into our session using `showtext::showtext_auto()`. A typical code chunk to do this could look like: ```{{r}} #| label: live-download-google-fonts ## Clean the slate systemfonts::clear_local_fonts() systemfonts::clear_registry() # Add three Google Fonts # Arguments: font family name, Google Font name font_add_google("Roboto Condensed", "Roboto Condensed") font_add_google("Lato", "Lato") font_add_google("Alegreya", "Alegreya") ## Enable these fonts showtext_auto() # set these fonts as default for the session ## Optional Check, comment out this line in production code sysfonts::font_families() # check which fonts are available in the session ``` Ensure that you use the right `name` for the font family, as shown above. It is text-sensitive. The `family` is up to you to choose. Using similar names for `name` and `family` is a good idea, as shown above. ### Option 2: Adding local fonts from your computer Using Google fonts as shown above means that every time someone loads your website on their browser, the browser goes off to Google to download the fonts on the fly. This will typically make your website non-compliant with GDPR (see below). One solution is to download fonts *a priori* from Google, or from elsewhere, and then import them into your session. The `sysfonts::font_add()` function allows us to do this. You will need to provide the path to the font files on your computer. That is our next step. Let's assume we have gone off to [Google Fonts](https://fonts.google.com/) and downloaded the following fonts :`Alegreya`,`Anton`, `Roboto Condensed`, `Schoolbell`, `Tangerine`, and `Ibarra Real Nova`. These font files are placed at `/fonts/`, i.e. a `fonts` folder at the root our our project. A code chunk to add these fonts to our R session as follows, using the `{{here}}` package: ```{{r}} #| label: add-local-fonts ## Clean the slate systemfonts::clear_local_fonts() systemfonts::clear_registry() ## showtext_opts(dpi = 96) # set DPI for showtext # First Add the Fonts sysfonts::font_add( family = "Alegreya", regular = here::here("fonts", "Alegreya-Regular.ttf"), bold = here::here("fonts", "Alegreya-Bold.ttf"), italic = here::here("fonts", "Alegreya-Italic.ttf"), bolditalic = here::here("fonts", "Alegreya-BoldItalic.ttf") ) sysfonts::font_add( family = "Anton", regular = here::here("fonts", "Anton-Regular.ttf") ) # Only one style is available sysfonts::font_add( family = "RobotoCondensed", regular = here::here("fonts", "RobotoCondensed-Regular.ttf"), bold = here::here("fonts", "RobotoCondensed-Bold.ttf"), italic = here::here("fonts", "RobotoCondensed-Italic.ttf"), bolditalic = here::here("fonts", "RobotoCondensed-BoldItalic.ttf") ) sysfonts::font_add( family = "IbarraNova", regular = here::here("fonts", "IbarraRealNova-Regular.ttf"), bold = here::here("fonts", "IbarraRealNova-Bold.ttf"), italic = here::here("fonts", "IbarraRealNova-Italic.ttf"), bolditalic = here::here("fonts", "IbarraRealNova-BoldItalic.ttf") ) sysfonts::font_add( family = "Tangerine", regular = here::here("fonts", "Tangerine-Regular.ttf"), bold = here::here("fonts", "Tangerine-Bold.ttf") ) # only these two are available sysfonts::font_add( family = "Schoolbell", regular = here::here("fonts", "Schoolbell-Regular.ttf") ) # Only regular is available ## Enable these fonts showtext_auto() # set these fonts as default for the session ## Optional Check, comment out this line in production code sysfonts::font_families() # check which fonts are available in the session ``` A couple of things worth knowing about the `{here}` package in R: - `here::here("fonts", "Alegreya-Regular.ttf")` **builds a path from your project root** (wherever here finds a `.Rproj`, `.here` file, or `.git` folder), not from the current script's location. So the fonts folder should just be `/fonts/`. - If your fonts folder isn't actually at the project root, adjust the first argument(s) accordingly, e.g. `here::here("assets", "fonts", "Alegreya-Regular.ttf")` if it's nested under `assets/` for example. - If you don't already have a .here marker or RStudio project file at the root you want here to anchor to, run `here::set_here()` once from that directory, or just open the project as an RStudio Project (.Rproj), which `{here}` will detect automatically. ## Plot Theme using Desired fonts Now that we have the fonts installed, either way, one more step remains: we need to set our ggplot theme to use these fonts. What are these `theme` elements? ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![ggplot2 Theme Elements. Source: Rosana Ferrero, on Twitter Sept 11, 2022](../../../../../materials/images/ggplot_theme_elements.jfif){#fig-ggplot-theme-elements fig-alt='ggplot2 Theme Elements. Source: Rosana Ferrero on Twitter, Sept 11, 2022'} ::: ::: So now that we understand the elements of the themes, let us set our ggplot theme: ### Setting fonts for ggplot themes First we set the fonts for the ***non-graphical*** elements in ggplot, such as `title`, `subtitle`, `axis title`, and `legend title` for example: ```{{r}} #| label: set-ggplot2-theme #| theme_custom <- function(){ theme_bw(base_size = 10) + # Base Theme, Black-White theme_sub_axis(title = element_text(family = "Roboto Condensed", size = 8), text = element_text(family = "Roboto Condensed", size = 6)) + theme_sub_legend(text = element_text(family = "Roboto Condensed", size = 6), title = element_text(family = "Montserrat", size = 8)) + theme_sub_plot(title = element_text(family = "Montserrat", size = 14, face = "bold"), title.position = "plot", subtitle = element_text(family = "Montserrat", size = 10), caption = element_text(family = "Montserrat", size = 6), caption.position = "plot") } ## Set the theme ggplot2::theme_set(new = theme_custom()) ``` ### Setting fonts for ggplot elements We now need to enable to use of these fonts ***inside*** the chart area of ggplot, say in `annotations`, `text` geoms, `label` geoms, and `marquee` geoms. ::: callout-note ### Fonts in ggplot Using `showtext(auto)` as shown above allows us to modify the ***non-graph*** elements of the ggplot chart: the `axes`, the `title`, the `legend` etc. If we wish to add text with fonts to the body of the chart itself, as with geoms such as `text`and `label` annotations , we need to do one more thing: use `update_geom_defaults()` as shown below: ::: ```{{r}} #| label: set-geom-default-font #| ## Use available fonts in ggplot label and text within the ggplot geoms ggplot2::update_geom_defaults(geom = "text", new = list( family = "Roboto Condensed", face = "plain", size = 3.5, color = "#2b2b2b" ) ) ggplot2::update_geom_defaults(geom = "label", new = list( family = "Roboto Condensed", face = "plain", size = 3.5, color = "#2b2b2b" ) ) ``` ## Final Step: Using the Fonts!! Where do we put all these code chunks floating around??!!! Quarto now has a feature that includes a`_setup.qmd` at the root of your Project. These code chunks, preferable in **one single code chunk**, can be pasted into this file, and this file invoked at the start of each new document using: `{{< include /_setup.qmd >}}` A sample `setup.qmd` format, with quite some detail, is embedded below: ```{{r}} #| label: setup-site #| include: false #| cache: false # Install/load packages if needed if (!requireNamespace("showtext", quietly = TRUE)) { install.packages("showtext") } if (!requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)) { install.packages("ggplot2") } library(showtext) library(ggplot2) # Add three Google Fonts # Arguments: font family name, Google Font name font_add_google("Roboto Condensed", "Roboto Condensed") font_add_google("Lato", "Lato") font_add_google("Alegreya", "Alegreya") # Tell R to use showtext for all subsequent plots showtext_auto() # Optional: set DPI for raster devices (adjust if you need high-res PNGs) showtext_opts(dpi = 300) # Set a site-wide ggplot theme using the loaded fonts ggplot2::theme_set( ggplot2::theme_bw( base_size = 14, base_family = "Roboto Condensed" ) ) ## Set the ggplot theme theme_madhatter <- function(base_size = 10, exhibit = TRUE) { th <- ggplot2::theme_bw(base_size = base_size) + ggplot2::theme( plot.margin = ggplot2::margin(t = 1, r = 2, b = 1, l = 1, unit = "cm"), axis.title = ggplot2::element_text( family = "Roboto Condensed", size = 10 ), axis.text = ggplot2::element_text( family = "Roboto Condensed", size = 8 ), legend.text = ggplot2::element_text( family = "Roboto Condensed", size = 6 ), legend.title = ggplot2::element_text( family = "Alegreya", size = 8 ), plot.title = ggplot2::element_text( family = "Alegreya", size = 14, face = "bold" ), plot.title.position = "plot", plot.subtitle = ggplot2::element_text( family = "Alegreya", size = 10 ), plot.caption = ggplot2::element_text( family = "Alegreya", size = 6 ), plot.caption.position = "plot" )} ## Set the theme for all plots ggplot2::theme_set(theme_madhatter()) ## Update the fonts for geoms as well! ggplot2::update_geom_defaults(geom = "text", new = list( family = "Roboto Condensed", face = "plain", size = 3.5, color = "#2b2b2b" ) ) ggplot2::update_geom_defaults(geom = "label", new = list( family = "Roboto Condensed", face = "plain", size = 3.5, color = "#2b2b2b" ) ) ``` NOTE: this code chunk is **all** that is in the file `_setup.qmd`. There is nothing else, no YAML header, no sections, no text. Just one code chunk. ## Does it all work?? Let us quickly see the results of using this `_setup.qmd`. We will compare a plain, basic plot, with one achieved after invoking `_setup.qmd`. #### Data We will work with a **familiar** dataset, so that we can concentrate on the chart aesthetics, without having to spend time getting used to the data: the `penguins` dataset again, now part of the R installation! ::: {#tbl-read-penguins-data .cell tbl-cap='Penguins Dataset'} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

And Here below, is the same chart achieved with the new theme, which was set using the `_setup.qmd()` from above: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![PLot themed with setup.qmd](https://project-peasants.netlify.app/classwork/day1/index_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){#fig-themed-ggplot} ::: ::: ## Using `{marquee}` To be written up when I know it better. ## Using `{ggtext}` From [Claus Wilke's website](https://wilkelab.org/ggtext/) → www.wilkelab.org/ggtext > The `ggtext` package provides simple Markdown and HTML rendering for ggplot2. Under the hood, the package uses the `gridtext` package for the actual rendering, and consequently it is limited to the feature set provided by `gridtext`. Support is provided for Markdown both in theme elements (plot titles, subtitles, captions, axis labels, legends, etc.) and in geoms (similar to `geom_text()`). In both cases, there are two alternatives, one for creating simple text labels and one for creating text boxes with word wrapping. NOTE: on some machines, the ggtext package may not work as expected. In this case, please do as follows, using your Console: - remove gridtext: `remove.packages(gridtext)`. - Install development version of `gridtext`: `remotes::install_github("wilkelab/gridtext")` ### `element_markdown()` We can use our familiar markdown syntax right inside the titles and captions of the plot. `element_markdown()` is a theming command made available by the `ggtext` package. `element_markdown()` → formatted text elements, e.g. titles, caption, axis text, striptext ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Set the theme ggplot2::theme_set(new = theme_custom()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error in `theme_custom()`: ! could not find function "theme_custom" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} p1 + ## New code starts here: Two Step Procedure with ggtext ## 1. Markdown formatting of labels and title, using asterisks labs( title = "Bill Dimensions of Brush-Tailed Penguins (*Pygoscelis*)", subtitle = "A scatter plot of bill depth versus bill length.", caption = "Data: Gorman, Williams & Fraser (2014) *PLoS ONE*", x = "**Bill Length** (mm)", y = "**Bill Depth** (mm)", color = "Body mass (g)" ) + ## 2. Add theme related commands from ggtext ## render respective text elements theme( plot.title = ggtext::element_markdown(), plot.caption = ggtext::element_markdown(), axis.title.x = ggtext::element_markdown(), axis.title.y = ggtext::element_markdown() ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error: ! object 'p1' not found ``` ::: ::: ### `element_markdown()` in combination with HTML This allows us to change fonts and font-effects in titles, labels, and captions: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## use HTML syntax to change text color p1 + labs(title = 'Bill Dimensions of Brush-Tailed Penguins Pygoscelis') + theme( plot.title = ggtext::element_markdown(), plot.caption = ggtext::element_markdown(), axis.title.x = ggtext::element_markdown(), axis.title.y = ggtext::element_markdown(), plot.margin = margin(t = 10, r = 10, b = 10, l = 10) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error: ! object 'p1' not found ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ## use HTML syntax to change font and text size ## p1 + labs(title = 'Bill Dimensions of Brush-Tailed Penguins Pygoscelis') + theme( plot.title = ggtext::element_markdown(), plot.caption = ggtext::element_markdown(), axis.title.x = ggtext::element_markdown(), axis.title.y = ggtext::element_markdown(), plot.margin = margin(t = 10, r = 10, b = 10, l = 10) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error: ! object 'p1' not found ``` ::: ::: ## Wait, but Why? - Using appropriate fonts in our plots can make them more readable and visually appealing. - They may be mandated for publication in some journals, and for publications by organizations. - Using `sysfonts` , `gfonts`, and `showtext` allows us to use a wide variety of fonts from Google, making it easy to customize our plots. - Using `ggtext` allows us to add formatted text elements to our plots, making them more informative and visually appealing. - Note that downloading fonts from Google may not be GDPR compliant, so it is better to use locally installed fonts if possible. - `gfonts` allows us to programmatically download Google fonts *a priori*, and use them locally, making our websites GDPR compliant. ## Conclusions In this module, we have learned how to use custom fonts in our ggplot2 plots using the `showtext` package. We have also seen how to use the `ggtext` package to add markdown-formatted text elements to our plots. ## References 1. Thomas Lin Pedersen. 1. Winston Chang. *R Cookbook* (2nd Edition).
